newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Mobutu's son says massacre warning "ridiculous nonsense".
newsitem.headline: Mobutu's son says massacre warning "ridiculous nonsense".

text.p: Zairean President Mobutu Sese Seko's son on Friday dismissed as "ridiculous nonsense" claims by rebels that his father had ordered a massacre of expatriates in Kinshasa in order to trigger a foreign intervention.
"This is pure intoxication. It is ridiculous nonsense. There's no foreigner here who will be killed by the government of Zaire, they are trying to spread panic," Nzanga Mobutu told Reuters.
Rebel leader Laurent Kabila accused Mobutu through an aide of ordering the massacre of all expatriates in the capital to provoke foreign intervention and avert his downfall.
In a statement to reporters in the second city of Lubumbashi Kabila sent the man he wants to be finance minister to give a warning that the alleged plot could "start at any minute".

"The AFDL (rebel alliance) has learned from very reliable sources that Mobutu and his team have charged his SARM (military intelligence) and DSP (presidential guard) to kill all the expatriates who live in Kinshasa," Mwana Nanga Mawanpanga said.

"In this way, they could put those killings on our forces which have not reached Kinshasa yet. And the reason for that is that they want to attract the intervention of foreign forces which are in Brazzaville (across the Zaire river in the Congo republic)," he added.
But Nzanga, who is also the president's spokesman, said the claims were absurd and were designed to spread panic in the Zairean capital, a city of more than five million people.
Diplomats said they received worried calls overnight from their home capitals after the predictions of an impending massacre of foreigners were broadcast.
"It is clearly designed to spread panic in Kinshasa and it is already succeeding in doing so," one Western diplomat said.
Kabila's forces have seized about half of Zaire's territory and he says they will reach the capital within three weeks.
The rebel leader on Friday hardened his tone over planned face-to-face talks with Mobutu, thus dimming hopes for averting war in the sprawling capital.
He told Reuters he had no time for protracted talks with Mobutu but would only attend a short ceremony on the transfer of power. Mobutu looked certain to reject this.
